Cavorite X7 to Become a Medical Aircraft for Northern Ontario Indigenous Communities
8 photos
Photo: Horizon Aircraft
While eVTOLs (electric vertical takeoff and landing) were originally developed with urban air mobility in mind, hybrid-electric VTOLs have immense potential for improving access to and from remote locations and communities, thanks to their extended range. The Canadian-made Cavorite X7 has exactly what it takes to provide lifesaving air services to Indigenous communities.
Constance Lake First Nation (CLFN) is an Oji-Cree and Cree community, whose members live on the shores of Constance Lake, close to Hearst in Northern Ontario. Despite the beauty and natural richness of the region, limited access to emergency medical transportation is one of the major setbacks. The geographical location and the harsh weather conditions make it difficult for critical patient transfer and deliveries to operate as they should.
A new agreement between CLFN and Horizon Aircraft is about to change that for the better. Based on this MoU, the Cavorite X7 could operate as a lifesaving medical aircraft for the community, although an official number of aircraft wasn’t yet specified.
The Cavorite X7 has what it takes to fulfill this difficult role. First, it has the speed and range to access these remote areas faster than conventional medevac helicopters, with no need for a dedicated runway.
Another important aspect that makes it better than conventional helicopters is the certified ability to operate in conditions of low visibility, snow, and extreme cold. This means it will be able to ensure critical air service year-round, in a region where bad weather is frequent and where such services are currently non-existent.
Although CLFN was the first to sign an official agreement to start operating Cavorite X7 aircraft, other Indigenous communities could eventually benefit from this as well. In fact, Horizon Aircraft Co-Founder and CEO Brandon Robinson believes that this Canadian-made, hybrid-electric VTOL could become “a national model” for better critical air mobility in remote communities.
One of the first hybrid-electric VTOLs ever made, the Cavorite X7 sports Sci-Fi-looking transforming wings that reveal 12 lift fans during the vertical takeoff, and then conceal them during the forward flight phase (that’s when they’re covered by sliding panels). This innovative fan-in-wing design improves speed, range, and harsh weather operations, compared to standard helicopters on one side, and open-rotor eVTOLs, on the other side.
The seven-seat configuration is another feature that sets apart the Cavorite X7. This was an upgrade from the original design, the Cavorite X5. Coupled with a range of up to 800 km/500 miles (mid-load, with fuel reserve) at a 450 kph/250 knots cruise speed, this configuration makes the Cavorite X7 one of the best options out there for regional air mobility.
The Canadian-made hybrid-electric VTOL is currently targeting Instrument Flight Rules (IFR) and Flight Into Known Icing (FIKI) certification, in partnership with the Flight Centre of Excellence and the University of Toronto.
